title: Saudi Arabia Warns of 'Firm' Response After Houthi Attacks Wound 13
excerpt: Riyadh vowed a firm response to Yemen's Houthis after ballistic missile and drone attacks on the kingdom's south, as emergency alerts rang across six cities including the Red Sea oil port of Yanbu.
body:
• Saudi Arabia warned on Tuesday it will react "firmly" to Yemen's Houthis after ballistic missile and drone attacks wounded 13 civilians in the country's south.
  • The Riyadh-led coalition confirmed strikes on Monday against Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif; the Houthis claimed a "large-scale" attack with dozens of missiles and drones on the King Khalid airbase.
  • Saudi Civil Defence issued emergency alerts in six cities, including the Red Sea oil port of Yanbu, before declaring the danger had passed.
  • The Houthis' politburo vowed its response "will continue and escalate," raising fears of a widening regional war.

Saudi Arabia warned on Tuesday that it will react "firmly" to Yemen's Houthis after a series of attacks carried out by the Iran-aligned rebels using ballistic missiles and drones wounded 13 civilians in the country's south.

The Riyadh-led coalition confirmed there had been missile and drone attacks the previous day on Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif. In a statement, the Houthi military said the strikes were retaliation for more than 100 Saudi airstrikes in Yemen over the past three days that it claimed had killed many people, and said it had fired "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones."

Attacks on the south

The Houthis claimed a new "large-scale" attack on the King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, in southern Saudi Arabia. The group said its missiles and drones hit aircraft hangars, radar systems, runways and ammunition depots at the base.

A resident of Khamis Mushait told AFP he heard "intense blasts" that left fires burning for a "long time." "Honestly, we couldn't sleep at all," he said. Riyadh answered the assault with more than 50 strikes, as it had the day before, according to the Houthis.

The attacks come a week after a major Houthi assault on four southern Saudi cities — Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran — that wounded 73 people, including women and children, and set oil installations ablaze in one of the biggest attacks on the kingdom since the US-Iran war began in February.

Alerts across the kingdom

Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence issued emergency alerts through the National Early Warning Platform for six cities amid the uptick in attacks, including Yanbu, the kingdom's main Red Sea oil port, where millions of barrels a day are loaded. Alerts also went out in Jeddah, Abha, Jazan, AlUla and Taif.

On Tuesday the Civil Defence sent an all-clear, saying the danger had passed in all six cities. The alerts underline how close the fighting has come to the kingdom's energy lifeline: Riyadh has rerouted most of its crude through Yanbu since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively shut.

"The coalition will deal with the attacks firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom and will take all necessary operational measures to deter this hostile and extremist approach."

— Saudi-led coalition statement

Escalation on both sides

Neither side is backing down. Hazem al-Assad of the Houthis' politburo said the "Yemeni response will continue and escalate as long as they (Saudi Arabia) persist in their aggression against our people."

The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with Saudi-backed government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Last week the group seized control of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait — which has become vital as the wider US-Iran war chokes the Strait of Hormuz — and over the weekend it captured the strategic Perim Island at the strait's mouth.

The fighting is already disrupting global energy flows. Commodity vessel transits at the Strait of Hormuz totaled four on Monday, down from 10 the previous day, according to preliminary Kpler data, and two oil tankers loaded with Saudi crude for China and India made U-turns in the Red Sea on Tuesday after Houthi warnings to shipping companies. Planned talks between Gulf Arab states and Iran in Oman were postponed.

Diaspora Angle

Saudi Arabia hosts one of the world's largest Indian expatriate communities, and a widening conflict puts the safety of millions of Indian workers — and the remittances their families depend on — directly at risk.

What's Next

The question now is what "firmly" means in practice: whether Riyadh launches a sustained air campaign against Houthi positions along the Red Sea coast, or seeks US military help, which sources told Reuters it has already requested. Either path risks turning a two-sided fight into a wider regional war.
